abstract: Body condition scoring can serve as an operational indicator of an animal's current welfare state and may also shed light on preceding, welfare-relevant conditions, such as stress. In farmed insects, limitations posed by the exoskeleton largely preclude traditional body condition assessment. However, adult black soldier flies (BSF) farmed in the insect protein industry have transparent abdominal panels that allow for visualisation of a portion of their fat body. Prior work has shown that the relative size of the fat body in the window, termed 'window fullness' (WF), at time of eclosion was reduced in adult females that were handled daily as prepupae (which also led to mortality, reduced body size, and developmental delays), suggesting it may predict prior stress. Accordingly, we investigated if WF correlated with relative lipid levels in newly emerged BSF; determined if assessors could score WF on an ordinal scale by eye; and assessed if WF changed when flies were pupated in non-preferred substrates. Relative lipid content strongly correlated with WF in males but not in females. Across all observers, WF could be scored by eye on an ordinal scale with 78.38% accuracy (range: 70.27 - 89.19%). Pupating in a preferred substrate correlated with increased dry mass and head widths for both sexes; females had increased WF (14.81%) but male WF was not affected. Overall, these data suggest WF could have promise as an on-farm-assessable indicator of body condition for BSF; however, there may be sex-specific differences in validity or reliability that require further investigation.
